subthemes.text:
OVERVIEW

[1] XXXX XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Mexico, is appealing the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) decision rejecting his refugee protection claim.

[2] The appellant states that he fears being killed by members of the Jalisco Nueva Generacion cartel (cartel) because he managed to escape after they had confined him for the purpose of recruiting him.

[3] The RPD found that the appellant was not credible due to discrepancies, inconsistencies and omissions in his testimony at the hearing and because of the lack of reasonable explanations.

[4] The appellant submits that the RPD erred in concluding that the differences between the Basis of Claim Form (BOC Form) and his testimony regarding the number of people present during his confinement undermined his credibility. The RPD also erred in concluding that he gave contradictory testimony regarding the contents of the house in which he was allegedly confined and the people who informed him that individuals from the cartel were lurking around his home.

ANALYSIS

[10] The RAD conducted an independent analysis of all the evidence, which included listening to the recording of the RPD hearing, and applied the correctness standard.4
CREDIBILITY
The appellant based his refugee protection claim on his cousin's written account and his testimony at the hearing

[11] In its decision, the RPD indicates that it asked the appellant and his cousin why their lives would be at risk if they returned to Mexico. They both alleged that they fear being killed by the cartel that wanted to recruit them. They claimed that they escaped after being kidnapped and confined. The appellant and his cousin testified that that was the only source of their fear. The RPD specifies that it then mainly put questions to the appellant's cousin and repeatedly told the appellant that he could supplement his cousin's testimony. The appellant allegedly responded each time that he had nothing to add and agreed with the testimony.

argument_evidence.context_text: [12] On listening to the recording of the hearing, the RAD did note that after the appellant's cousin testified in detail about their kidnapping, confinement and escape, and the information that suspicious cars were driving around their former residence, the RPD asked the appellant whether he had anything to add.
He replied no and stated that he completely agreed with his cousin's testimony.

[13] The RAD considers that the evidence demonstrates that the appellant based his refugee protection claim on that of his cousin and that he clearly agreed with his cousin's testimony at the RPD hearing.
He did not mention the presence of five cartel members because he did not think it was important.

It rejected the explanation that the word [translation] "alone" in the written account meant "alone" in relation to the cartel because it is specifically stated that the cartel members returned after leaving them "alone.

[19] Having noted that the kidnapping and confinement of the appellant and his cousin formed the basis of the written account, the RPD found that their credibility was undermined, and it concluded that, on a balance of probabilities, they did not establish that they had been kidnapped and confined by cartel members.

subthemes.text:
[12] On listening to the recording of the hearing, the RAD did note that after the appellant's cousin testified in detail about their kidnapping, confinement and escape, and the information that suspicious cars were driving around their former residence, the RPD asked the appellant whether he had anything to add. He replied no and stated that he completely agreed with his cousin's testimony.5 At the end of the hearing, the RPD asked him whether he had anything to add, and he reiterated that he agreed with what his cousin had stated.6

[13] The RAD considers that the evidence demonstrates that the appellant based his refugee protection claim on that of his cousin and that he clearly agreed with his cousin's testimony at the RPD hearing.
Circumspection is required when making a negative credibility finding

[14] The appellant submits in his memorandum that the panel must exercise caution when making finding of a lack of credibility. The RAD shares this point of view. As stated by the Federal Court in Maldonado,7 when a refugee protection claimant swears that certain facts are true, this creates a presumption that they are true unless there is valid reason to doubt their truthfulness. In this case, the RAD is of the opinion that the RPD had reasons to doubt their truthfulness.
Appellant's job

[15] The RAD did not note any errors and agrees with the RPD's unchallenged conclusion that the appellant did not establish that he had worked with his cousin in a garage. That undermines the credibility of the written account, which states that he was kidnapped with his cousin at the end of their workday in a garage.
Contradictions regarding the confinement conditions

[16] According to the written account of the appellant's cousin,8 he was alone with the appellant for a few days during their confinement:
[Translation]
They took us by force and put us in the car with a bag over our heads. After about 40-50 minutes, they brought us into a house. We were blindfolded; they did not give us any food or water and left us there. We were alone for a few days. When they returned, they wanted us to work for them. They are part of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel. This cartel recruits young people like us to work in their organization. If we did not do so, they threatened to kill us and our families. They hit us several times. They left. I managed to untie myself and my cousin. We broke a window and managed to escape. [emphasis added]

[17] The RPD points out that, at the hearing, the appellant's cousin testified that five cartel members had kept watch on them for three days and that on the fourth day, only one remained. He stated that during their confinement, the cartel members allegedly beat them, struck them in the face and hit them with their weapons. The RPD asked the appellant's cousin why the BOC Form states that they were [translation] "alone." He replied that he meant [translation] "alone" with the cartel members. He did not mention the presence of five cartel members because he did not think it was important.

[18] The RPD did not consider these explanations reasonable. It rejected the explanation that the word [translation] "alone" in the written account meant "alone" in relation to the cartel because it is specifically stated that the cartel members returned after leaving them "alone." The RPD also rejected the explanation that it was not important to mention the fact that five cartel members had been keeping watch on them and beating them. Since the written account states that the appellant and his cousin were deprived of food and water and beaten when the cartel members returned, the RPD would have expected it to mention the presence of five cartel members and the fact that they were beaten throughout their confinement.

[19] Having noted that the kidnapping and confinement of the appellant and his cousin formed the basis of the written account, the RPD found that their credibility was undermined, and it concluded that, on a balance of probabilities, they did not establish that they had been kidnapped and confined by cartel members.

[27] The RAD is of the opinion that the contradiction between the appellant's cousin's written account and his testimony, without satisfactory explanations as to the people present during his confinement and that of the appellant, goes to the core of their story and undermines the appellant's credibility.

subthemes.text:
[20] In his memorandum, the appellant claims that the inconsistency noted by the RPD concerns whether cartel members were present during his confinement. He alleges that [translation] "what is written and what was stated during testimony is consistent, the words were just misinterpreted." According to the appellant, there is no real discrepancy between the two versions, they complement each other and are consistent. The appellant claims that since he and his cousin were blindfolded, it is normal for them to be confused as to the number of people who were present in the house and the length of time spent there.

[21] The RAD agrees with the RPD's point of view. It does not accept the arguments made by the appellant in his memorandum. It considers that there is a clear discrepancy between the appellant's cousin's written account and his testimony at the hearing. It is of the opinion that these versions are not consistent and do not complement each other. Like the RPD, it is not of the opinion that the appellant's cousin's explanations are satisfactory.

[22] On listening to the recording of the hearing, the RAD noted that the RPD correctly related the appellant's cousin's testimony. The appellant's cousin testified that cartel members were allegedly present in the house throughout the period during which they were confined, which is inconsistent with the version given in the written account. The appellant's cousin indicated that there were allegedly five people.9 They were apparently present for XXXX days, and on the XXXX day, only one had stayed behind, and they apparently managed to escape that day.10 The leader of the cartel members reportedly arrived at the house on the XXXX or XXXX day-it was in the early morning hours-and the five people who had kidnapped them were in the house before he arrived.11

[23] The RAD also noted that at the hearing, the appellant's cousin stated12 that they were beaten throughout the period of their confinement. He stated that he was hit with weapons, kicked and punched all over his body; he was also allegedly struck in the face, and traumatizing language was used. The appellant was also allegedly beaten. In contrast, the appellant's cousin's written account indicates that when the cartel members returned after having left them alone, they allegedly demanded that they work with them, struck them several times, and left.

[24] The RAD does not consider the appellant's cousin's explanations given at the hearing to be satisfactory. The word [translation] "alone" used in the context of the written account leaves no room for interpretation, as the appellant claims: [Translation] "We were alone for a few days. When they returned..." It is clear that this cannot mean [translation] "alone" in relation to the cartel members, since the next sentence precisely alludes to the cartel members' return, which inevitably leads to the inference that they had not been there until then.

[25] In addition, the RAD is of the opinion that it is inconsistent that the appellant did not think it important to mention the presence of five cartel members. If the appellant and his cousin were beaten throughout the period of their confinement, the RAD cannot understand why they did not mention it and why they also failed to mention the presence of the five people who beat them. As stated in the BOC Form, a refugee protection claimant is required to include everything that is important for their refugee protection claim in this form.

[26] In addition, the RAD does not accept the explanation given by the appellant in his memorandum that the appellant and his cousin were confused as to the number of people present in the house because they were blindfolded. At no point during the hearing did the RAD note any such confusion, quite the opposite, the appellant's cousin stated without hesitation that the five people who kidnapped them were present and that a commander then arrived in the early morning hours, and a little later, only one member of the cartel was left. Furthermore, the RAD did not note any confusion in the written account, which is equally affirmative, but this time in support of the fact that the appellant and his cousin had been alone in the house for a few days.

[27] The RAD is of the opinion that the contradiction between the appellant's cousin's written account and his testimony, without satisfactory explanations as to the people present during his confinement and that of the appellant, goes to the core of their story and undermines the appellant's credibility. The RAD considers this contradiction determinative.

[28] The RAD concludes that, on a balance of probabilities, the appellant's kidnapping and confinement did not happen.

[29] The RAD considers the RPD's conclusion in this regard to be correct.
Contents of the house in which the appellant was allegedly confined and the presence of vehicles near his home

[30] In light of the aforementioned conclusion regarding the confinement conditions, the RAD does not consider it necessary to analyze the appellant's arguments regarding the RPD's alleged error in criticizing the appellant's cousin for his contradictory testimony at the hearing regarding the objects that were in the house where he was confined with the appellant.

REASONS FOR DECISION
OVERVIEW
[1] XXXX XXXX XXXX, a citizen of Mexico, is appealing the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) decision rejecting his refugee protection claim.

[2] The appellant states that he fears being killed by members of the Jalisco Nueva Generacion cartel (cartel) because he managed to escape after they had confined him for the purpose of recruiting him.
[3] The RPD found that the appellant was not credible due to discrepancies, inconsistencies and omissions in his testimony at the hearing and because of the lack of reasonable explanations.

[4] The appellant submits that the RPD erred in concluding that the differences between the Basis of Claim Form (BOC Form) and his testimony regarding the number of people present during his confinement undermined his credibility. The RPD also erred in concluding that he gave contradictory testimony regarding the contents of the house in which he was allegedly confined and the people who informed him that individuals from the cartel were lurking around his home.
[5] The Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) is of the view that the determinative issue is credibility.
[6] The RAD confirms the RPD's determination and dismisses the appeal.
BACKGROUND

[7] The RPD heard the appellant's refugee protection claim and that of his cousin, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (cousin), at the same time. It rejected the refugee protection claims on the same grounds. The appellant's cousin abandoned his appeal before the RAD.1

[8] According to the appellant's cousin's written account,2 on which the appellant bases his claim in his BOC Form,3 on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019, they were both kidnapped and confined for a few days by cartel members. They allegedly managed to escape. Neighbours reportedly informed them that they had noticed suspicious cars passing by their former residence.
[9] The appellant and his cousin allegedly left Mexico on XXXX XXXX XXXX 2019. They reportedly arrived in Canada the same day and claimed refugee protection here.
ANALYSIS

[10] The RAD conducted an independent analysis of all the evidence, which included listening to the recording of the RPD hearing, and applied the correctness standard.4
CREDIBILITY
The appellant based his refugee protection claim on his cousin's written account and his testimony at the hearing

[11] In its decision, the RPD indicates that it asked the appellant and his cousin why their lives would be at risk if they returned to Mexico. They both alleged that they fear being killed by the cartel that wanted to recruit them. They claimed that they escaped after being kidnapped and confined. The appellant and his cousin testified that that was the only source of their fear. The RPD specifies that it then mainly put questions to the appellant's cousin and repeatedly told the appellant that he could supplement his cousin's testimony. The appellant allegedly responded each time that he had nothing to add and agreed with the testimony.

[12] On listening to the recording of the hearing, the RAD did note that after the appellant's cousin testified in detail about their kidnapping, confinement and escape, and the information that suspicious cars were driving around their former residence, the RPD asked the appellant whether he had anything to add. He replied no and stated that he completely agreed with his cousin's testimony.5 At the end of the hearing, the RPD asked him whether he had anything to add, and he reiterated that he agreed with what his cousin had stated.6

[13] The RAD considers that the evidence demonstrates that the appellant based his refugee protection claim on that of his cousin and that he clearly agreed with his cousin's testimony at the RPD hearing.
Circumspection is required when making a negative credibility finding

[14] The appellant submits in his memorandum that the panel must exercise caution when making finding of a lack of credibility. The RAD shares this point of view. As stated by the Federal Court in Maldonado,7 when a refugee protection claimant swears that certain facts are true, this creates a presumption that they are true unless there is valid reason to doubt their truthfulness. In this case, the RAD is of the opinion that the RPD had reasons to doubt their truthfulness.
Appellant's job

[15] The RAD did not note any errors and agrees with the RPD's unchallenged conclusion that the appellant did not establish that he had worked with his cousin in a garage. That undermines the credibility of the written account, which states that he was kidnapped with his cousin at the end of their workday in a garage.
Contradictions regarding the confinement conditions

[16] According to the written account of the appellant's cousin,8 he was alone with the appellant for a few days during their confinement:
[Translation]
They took us by force and put us in the car with a bag over our heads. After about 40-50 minutes, they brought us into a house. We were blindfolded; they did not give us any food or water and left us there. We were alone for a few days. When they returned, they wanted us to work for them. They are part of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel. This cartel recruits young people like us to work in their organization. If we did not do so, they threatened to kill us and our families. They hit us several times. They left. I managed to untie myself and my cousin. We broke a window and managed to escape. [emphasis added]

[17] The RPD points out that, at the hearing, the appellant's cousin testified that five cartel members had kept watch on them for three days and that on the fourth day, only one remained. He stated that during their confinement, the cartel members allegedly beat them, struck them in the face and hit them with their weapons. The RPD asked the appellant's cousin why the BOC Form states that they were [translation] "alone." He replied that he meant [translation] "alone" with the cartel members. He did not mention the presence of five cartel members because he did not think it was important.

[18] The RPD did not consider these explanations reasonable. It rejected the explanation that the word [translation] "alone" in the written account meant "alone" in relation to the cartel because it is specifically stated that the cartel members returned after leaving them "alone." The RPD also rejected the explanation that it was not important to mention the fact that five cartel members had been keeping watch on them and beating them. Since the written account states that the appellant and his cousin were deprived of food and water and beaten when the cartel members returned, the RPD would have expected it to mention the presence of five cartel members and the fact that they were beaten throughout their confinement.

[19] Having noted that the kidnapping and confinement of the appellant and his cousin formed the basis of the written account, the RPD found that their credibility was undermined, and it concluded that, on a balance of probabilities, they did not establish that they had been kidnapped and confined by cartel members.

[20] In his memorandum, the appellant claims that the inconsistency noted by the RPD concerns whether cartel members were present during his confinement. He alleges that [translation] "what is written and what was stated during testimony is consistent, the words were just misinterpreted." According to the appellant, there is no real discrepancy between the two versions, they complement each other and are consistent. The appellant claims that since he and his cousin were blindfolded, it is normal for them to be confused as to the number of people who were present in the house and the length of time spent there.

[21] The RAD agrees with the RPD's point of view. It does not accept the arguments made by the appellant in his memorandum. It considers that there is a clear discrepancy between the appellant's cousin's written account and his testimony at the hearing. It is of the opinion that these versions are not consistent and do not complement each other. Like the RPD, it is not of the opinion that the appellant's cousin's explanations are satisfactory.

[22] On listening to the recording of the hearing, the RAD noted that the RPD correctly related the appellant's cousin's testimony. The appellant's cousin testified that cartel members were allegedly present in the house throughout the period during which they were confined, which is inconsistent with the version given in the written account. The appellant's cousin indicated that there were allegedly five people.9 They were apparently present for XXXX days, and on the XXXX day, only one had stayed behind, and they apparently managed to escape that day.10 The leader of the cartel members reportedly arrived at the house on the XXXX or XXXX day-it was in the early morning hours-and the five people who had kidnapped them were in the house before he arrived.11

[23] The RAD also noted that at the hearing, the appellant's cousin stated12 that they were beaten throughout the period of their confinement. He stated that he was hit with weapons, kicked and punched all over his body; he was also allegedly struck in the face, and traumatizing language was used. The appellant was also allegedly beaten. In contrast, the appellant's cousin's written account indicates that when the cartel members returned after having left them alone, they allegedly demanded that they work with them, struck them several times, and left.

[24] The RAD does not consider the appellant's cousin's explanations given at the hearing to be satisfactory. The word [translation] "alone" used in the context of the written account leaves no room for interpretation, as the appellant claims: [Translation] "We were alone for a few days. When they returned..." It is clear that this cannot mean [translation] "alone" in relation to the cartel members, since the next sentence precisely alludes to the cartel members' return, which inevitably leads to the inference that they had not been there until then.

[25] In addition, the RAD is of the opinion that it is inconsistent that the appellant did not think it important to mention the presence of five cartel members. If the appellant and his cousin were beaten throughout the period of their confinement, the RAD cannot understand why they did not mention it and why they also failed to mention the presence of the five people who beat them. As stated in the BOC Form, a refugee protection claimant is required to include everything that is important for their refugee protection claim in this form.

[26] In addition, the RAD does not accept the explanation given by the appellant in his memorandum that the appellant and his cousin were confused as to the number of people present in the house because they were blindfolded. At no point during the hearing did the RAD note any such confusion, quite the opposite, the appellant's cousin stated without hesitation that the five people who kidnapped them were present and that a commander then arrived in the early morning hours, and a little later, only one member of the cartel was left. Furthermore, the RAD did not note any confusion in the written account, which is equally affirmative, but this time in support of the fact that the appellant and his cousin had been alone in the house for a few days.

[27] The RAD is of the opinion that the contradiction between the appellant's cousin's written account and his testimony, without satisfactory explanations as to the people present during his confinement and that of the appellant, goes to the core of their story and undermines the appellant's credibility. The RAD considers this contradiction determinative.
[28] The RAD concludes that, on a balance of probabilities, the appellant's kidnapping and confinement did not happen.

[29] The RAD considers the RPD's conclusion in this regard to be correct.
Contents of the house in which the appellant was allegedly confined and the presence of vehicles near his home

[30] In light of the aforementioned conclusion regarding the confinement conditions, the RAD does not consider it necessary to analyze the appellant's arguments regarding the RPD's alleged error in criticizing the appellant's cousin for his contradictory testimony at the hearing regarding the objects that were in the house where he was confined with the appellant.

[31] For the same reason, the RAD does not consider it necessary to analyze the appellant's claim that the RPD should have accepted the explanation that neighbours informed their relatives that cartel individuals were lurking around their house.
[32] The RAD is of the view that the appellant's arguments outlined above are peripheral in light of the conclusion regarding the issue of the confinement conditions.
[33] The RAD concludes that the RPD's decision is correct.
CONCLUSION

[34] The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the RPD's determination, namely, that the appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.
(signed)
Isabelle Parizeau
Me Isabelle Parizeau
March 10, 2021
